prompt: Which statement correctly pairs each alkyne hydration method with its regiochemistry?

choices.text: Mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration gives the Markovnikov product; hydroboration–oxidation gives the non-Markovnikov product
Mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration gives the non-Markovnikov product; hydroboration–oxidation gives the Markovnikov product
choices.why: That is reversed. Direct, mercury(II)-catalyzed addition of water is Markovnikov; the indirect hydroboration–oxidation route is non-Markovnikov.

choices.text: Both methods give the Markovnikov product
choices.why: Hydroboration–oxidation is the indirect method, and it gives the non-Markovnikov product.

choices.text: Both methods give the non-Markovnikov product
choices.why: Direct addition of water catalyzed by mercury(II) ion follows Markovnikov's rule.

explanation: Like alkenes, alkynes can be hydrated two ways. Direct addition of water catalyzed by mercury(II) ion gives the Markovnikov product, and indirect addition of water by hydroboration–oxidation gives the non-Markovnikov product.

prompt: Why is mercury(II) sulfate added when an alkyne is hydrated with aqueous acid?

choices.text: Alkynes don't react with aqueous acid alone; HgSO4 is a Lewis acid catalyst
It reduces the alkyne to an alkene, which can then add water directly
choices.why: Hg^2+ isn't acting as a reducing agent. It adds to the alkyne as an electrophile, which starts the hydration.

choices.text: It supplies the oxygen atom that ends up in the ketone product
choices.why: The oxygen comes from water, which reacts with the vinylic cation. HgSO4 is the catalyst.

choices.text: It shifts the keto–enol equilibrium toward the enol so it can be isolated
choices.why: The equilibrium lies on the side of the ketone, and enols are almost never isolated.

explanation: Alkynes don't react directly with aqueous acid, but they undergo hydration readily in the presence of mercury(II) sulfate as a Lewis acid catalyst. Mercury(II) ion adds to the alkyne, water attacks, and the reaction goes on to a ketone.

prompt: What product is isolated when 1-hexyne is treated with H2O, H2SO4 and HgSO4?

choices.why: An aldehyde would mean the oxygen went to the terminal carbon (non-Markovnikov). Mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov.
This enol is an intermediate, but it immediately tautomerizes to the ketone. Enols are almost never isolated.
Hydration adds one H2O to the triple bond. The enol then rearranges to a C=O compound; no extra hydrogen is added.

explanation: Markovnikov addition puts the –OH on C2, the more highly substituted carbon, giving the enol CH2=C(OH)CH2CH2CH2CH3. The enol immediately tautomerizes, so the product isolated is the ketone 2-hexanone (78% in the section's example).

prompt: In the section's example, what percent yield of 2-hexanone is obtained by mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration of 1-hexyne?
explanation: 1-Hexyne with H2O, H2SO4 and HgSO4 gives an enol intermediate that tautomerizes to 2-hexanone, isolated in 78% yield.

prompt: Why is the enol formed in alkyne hydration almost never isolated?

choices.text: It rearranges at once, and the keto–enol equilibrium lies on the side of the ketone
It loses water and re-forms the alkyne
choices.why: The enol doesn't go back to the alkyne. It rearranges to its keto tautomer by a change in the position of a hydrogen.

choices.text: It is reduced to an alcohol under the reaction conditions
choices.why: Nothing reduces the enol. It isomerizes to the ketone, which is the product isolated.

choices.text: The equilibrium favors the enol, but the enol is too reactive to collect
choices.why: With few exceptions the keto–enol equilibrium lies on the side of the ketone.

explanation: An enol (ene + ol) is a vinylic alcohol. It is an intermediate in alkyne hydration, but it immediately rearranges into a ketone by keto–enol tautomerism. With few exceptions the equilibrium lies on the side of the ketone, so enols are almost never isolated.

prompt: Which pair of compounds are tautomers?

choices.why: These aren't isomers: the alcohol has two more hydrogens (C3H8O versus C3H6O). Tautomers are isomers that differ in the position of a hydrogen.
The enol is C3H6O but the alcohol is C3H8O, so they aren't isomers.
These isomers differ in geometry, not in the position of a hydrogen, and they don't interconvert spontaneously.

explanation: Tautomers are two isomers that undergo spontaneous interconversion accompanied by a change in the position of a hydrogen. The enol CH2=C(OH)CH3 and the ketone CH3COCH3 are an enol–keto pair: moving the hydrogen from oxygen to carbon turns C=C–OH into H–C–C=O.

prompt: What is the first step in the mechanism of mercury(II)-catalyzed alkyne hydration?

choices.text: Electrophilic addition of Hg^2+ to the alkyne, giving a vinylic cation
Addition of water to the alkyne, giving the enol directly
choices.why: Water reacts only after Hg^2+ has added and formed a vinylic cation.

choices.text: Tautomerization of the alkyne to an enol
choices.why: Tautomerization is the last step, and it turns the enol into the ketone.

choices.text: Reduction of a mercury compound with NaBH4
choices.why: No NaBH4 is used in alkyne hydration. The acidic conditions remove the mercury.

explanation: Figure 9.4.1: electrophilic addition of mercury(II) ion to the alkyne gives a vinylic cation, which reacts with water and loses a proton to give a mercury-containing enol. The acidic conditions replace the mercury with hydrogen, and tautomerization gives the ketone.

prompt: How does mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration of an alkyne differ from oxymercuration of an alkene?

choices.text: No NaBH4 step is needed; the acidic conditions alone replace mercury with hydrogen
It gives the non-Markovnikov product, with –OH on the less substituted carbon
choices.why: Both reactions are Markovnikov: the –OH goes to the more highly substituted carbon.

choices.text: It goes through no mercury-containing intermediate at any stage
choices.why: It does: water adds to the vinylic cation to give a mercury-containing enol.

choices.text: It needs two separate NaBH4 treatments to remove all the mercury
choices.why: No NaBH4 is needed at all in the alkyne reaction.

explanation: The mechanism is analogous to alkene oxymercuration (Section 8.4), but no treatment with NaBH4 is needed to remove the mercury. The acidic reaction conditions alone replace mercury by hydrogen, and the enol then tautomerizes to the ketone.

prompt: Why is mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration most useful for terminal alkynes, RC≡CH?

choices.text: Only a methyl ketone forms; unsymmetrical internal alkynes give ketone mixtures
Internal alkynes don't react at all with HgSO4 and aqueous acid
choices.why: Internal alkynes do react. The problem is that an unsymmetrical one gives both possible ketones.

choices.text: Terminal alkynes give an aldehyde, which is easier to isolate than a ketone
choices.why: Markovnikov hydration of a terminal alkyne gives a methyl ketone. Aldehydes come from hydroboration–oxidation.

choices.text: Only terminal alkynes go through an enol intermediate before the ketone forms
choices.why: Internal alkynes go through enols too. The difference is how many ketones can form.

explanation: A mixture of both possible ketones results when an unsymmetrically substituted internal alkyne (RC≡CR′) is hydrated. With a terminal alkyne, Markovnikov addition always puts the oxygen on the inner carbon, so only a methyl ketone forms.

prompt: What would you obtain by mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration of 4-octyne, CH3CH2CH2C≡CCH2CH2CH3?

choices.why: The oxygen ends up on one of the alkyne carbons, C4 or C5, and both choices give the same ketone. A ketone at C3 can't form.
An aldehyde needs the C=O at the end of the chain. The triple bond in 4-octyne is in the middle, so a ketone forms.
The enol tautomerizes to a ketone; no alcohol is formed.

explanation: 4-Octyne is symmetrical: each alkyne carbon carries a propyl group. Whichever carbon gets the oxygen, the product is the same ketone, 4-octanone (Exercise 9.4.1a). Only unsymmetrical internal alkynes give mixtures.

prompt: How many different ketones form when 2-hexyne, CH3C≡CCH2CH2CH2CH3, undergoes mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration?
explanation: 2-Hexyne is an unsymmetrically substituted internal alkyne: C2 carries a methyl group and C3 a propyl group. The oxygen can end up on either carbon, so a mixture of two ketones forms: 2-hexanone and 3-hexanone.

prompt: What does mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration of 2-methyl-4-octyne, (CH3)2CHCH2C≡CCH2CH2CH3, give?

choices.why: The two alkyne carbons carry different groups (an isobutyl and a propyl group), so the oxygen can go to either one and both ketones form.
Neither alkyne carbon is favored over the other, so both ketones form.
Hydration of an alkyne gives ketones, by tautomerization of the enol, not alcohols.

explanation: 2-Methyl-4-octyne is an unsymmetrical internal alkyne, so hydration gives both possible ketones. Oxygen on C4 gives (CH3)2CHCH2COCH2CH2CH2CH3, 2-methyl-4-octanone; oxygen on C5 gives (CH3)2CHCH2CH2COCH2CH2CH3, 7-methyl-4-octanone (Exercise 9.4.1b).

prompt: Which alkyne would you hydrate with HgSO4 and aqueous acid to make 2-pentanone, CH3COCH2CH2CH3, as the only product?

choices.why: 2-Pentyne is an unsymmetrical internal alkyne, so it would give a mixture of 2-pentanone and 3-pentanone.
Hydration adds no carbons. 1-Butyne would give a four-carbon methyl ketone.
This terminal alkyne has a branched chain, so its methyl ketone would be CH3COCH(CH3)2, not 2-pentanone.

explanation: A terminal alkyne gives only a methyl ketone on mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration. 2-Pentanone is the methyl ketone of an unbranched five-carbon chain, so the alkyne is 1-pentyne (Exercise 9.4.2a).

prompt: When BH3 is used to hydroborate a terminal alkyne, how many molecules of borane often add to the triple bond?
explanation: Hydroboration of a terminal alkyne is complicated because two molecules of borane often add to the triple bond. A bulky borane such as disiamylborane is used in place of BH3 to prevent this double addition.

prompt: Why is disiamylborane used instead of BH3 to hydroborate a terminal alkyne?

choices.text: Its bulk hinders a second addition, so only one borane adds to the triple bond
It reverses the regiochemistry to give the Markovnikov product
choices.why: Hydroboration–oxidation is non-Markovnikov either way. The bulky borane is used to stop double addition.

choices.text: Its vinylic borane doesn't need to be oxidized with H2O2
choices.why: The vinylic borane is still oxidized with H2O2 to give the enol.

choices.text: It adds only to internal alkynes, which avoids the terminal carbon
choices.why: Disiamylborane is used specifically with terminal alkynes, where BH3 often adds twice.

explanation: Bis(1,2-dimethylpropyl)borane, known as disiamylborane, is a bulky, sterically encumbered borane. With a terminal alkyne, its first addition to the triple bond occurs normally, but a second addition is hindered by its bulk. Oxidation with H2O2 then gives an enol, which tautomerizes to an aldehyde.

prompt: What is the product of hydroboration–oxidation (BH3, then H2O2) of 3-hexyne, CH3CH2C≡CCH2CH3?

choices.why: Aldehydes come from terminal alkynes. The triple bond of 3-hexyne is internal, so a ketone forms.
Oxidation of the vinylic borane gives an enol, which tautomerizes to a ketone, not an alcohol.
3-Hexyne is symmetrical. The oxygen goes on C3 or C4, and both give the same ketone; 2-hexanone can't form.

explanation: Hydroboration–oxidation of an internal alkyne such as 3-hexyne is straightforward and gives a ketone. The vinylic borane is oxidized by H2O2 to an enol, which tautomerizes to 3-hexanone.

prompt: 1-Hexyne is treated with disiamylborane and then with H2O2. What is the product?

choices.why: The methyl ketone comes from mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration. Hydroboration–oxidation puts the oxygen on the terminal carbon.
Oxidation gives an enol, which tautomerizes to an aldehyde; no alcohol is formed.
That enol is the intermediate. It tautomerizes to the aldehyde.

explanation: Hydroboration–oxidation is non-Markovnikov, so the oxygen goes to the terminal carbon. The enol formed by H2O2 oxidation tautomerizes to the aldehyde, hexanal. This complements mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration, which turns the same terminal alkyne into a methyl ketone.

prompt: Which alkyne would you start with to prepare C6H5CH2CHO by hydroboration–oxidation?

choices.why: Hydroboration–oxidation adds no carbons, so this alkyne would give C6H5CH2CH2CHO, with one CH2 too many.
An internal alkyne gives a ketone, not an aldehyde.
An internal alkyne gives a ketone. An aldehyde needs a terminal alkyne.

explanation: An aldehyde comes from hydroboration–oxidation of a terminal alkyne, with the CHO carbon coming from the terminal ≡CH. C6H5CH2CHO has two carbons attached to the ring, so the alkyne is C6H5C≡CH, phenylacetylene (Exercise 9.4.3a).

prompt: Which alkyne would you hydroborate and oxidize to make 2,5-dimethyl-3-hexanone, (CH3)2CHCOCH2CH(CH3)2, as the only product?

choices.why: A terminal alkyne gives an aldehyde by hydroboration–oxidation, and this one has too few carbons.
This alkyne is missing a methyl group, and because it is unsymmetrical it would give two ketones.
Hydroboration–oxidation of an alkene gives an alcohol. The enol route to a ketone needs an alkyne.

explanation: 2,5-Dimethyl-3-hexyne is a symmetrical internal alkyne, so whichever carbon receives the oxygen, the enol tautomerizes to the same ketone, 2,5-dimethyl-3-hexanone (Exercise 9.4.3b).

prompt: How would you convert cyclopentylacetylene, C5H9C≡CH (a cyclopentane ring bonded to –C≡CH), into the aldehyde C5H9CH2CHO?

choices.text: Hydroboration with disiamylborane, then oxidation with H2O2
Hydration with H2O, H2SO4 and HgSO4 as catalyst
choices.why: Mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration of a terminal alkyne gives the methyl ketone, C5H9COCH3, not the aldehyde.

choices.text: Hydration with H2O and H2SO4, leaving out the HgSO4
choices.why: Alkynes don't react directly with aqueous acid. The mercury(II) catalyst is needed, and even then the product would be a methyl ketone.

choices.text: Hydroboration with disiamylborane, with no H2O2 oxidation
choices.why: The vinylic borane must be oxidized by H2O2 to give the enol that tautomerizes to the aldehyde.

explanation: Hydroboration–oxidation of a terminal alkyne gives an aldehyde, while mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration of the same alkyne gives a methyl ketone. So C5H9CH2CHO comes from hydroboration–oxidation of cyclopentylacetylene (Exercise 9.4.4b).
